interest: Documents Japan's wartime control of religious bodies under the 1939 Religious Organizations Law and overtures to Islam.
overview: This file (U.S. State Department decimal file 894.404) encompasses diplomatic despatches, internal memoranda, intelligence reports, and correspondence from February 1932 to July 1939 documenting religious policy, institutions, and state-religion relations in imperial Japan and its expanding empire. The records trace the Japanese government's evolving management of religious life leading up to World War II, examining state investigations into the religious versus civic status of Shrine Shinto, the flourishing of sectarian movements like Tenrikyo, and church-state accommodations involving Roman Catholic and Protestant missions—highlighted by Cardinal Dougherty’s 1937 imperial audience and visit to the Meiji Shrine. The file also charts imperial Japan's geopolitical outreach toward the Islamic world, marked by the 1938 opening of Tokyo's first mosque, international Muslim delegations, and ensuing protests over statutory discrimination. The collection culminates in extensive reporting, diplomatic analysis, and a full official English translation of the Religious Organizations Law of 1939 (Law No. 77 of 1939), which centralized administrative supervision over Buddhist, Shinto, and Christian bodies under the Ministry of Education.
